items.description: Invitation Homes Announces Addition of M. Colin Connolly to Board of Directors 11/11/2026 Download (opens in new window) DALLAS--(BUSINESS WIRE)-- Invitation Homes Inc. (NYSE: INVH) (“Invitation Homes” or the “Company”), the nation’s premier single-family home leasing and management company, today announced that M. Colin Connolly, President, Chief Executive Officer, and Director of Cousins Properties Incorporated (“Cousins”) has been appointed to the Company’s board of directors (the “Board”), effective November 13, 2026. Mr. Connolly, who the Board has determined is independent, will serve on the Compensation and Management Development Committee and the Investment and Finance Committee. His appointment increases the size of the Board to ten members. “Colin brings a fresh perspective from leading another public REIT through multiple market cycles,” said Michael Fascitelli, Chairperson of the Board. “His leadership and vast real estate experience will strengthen the Board’s discussions, and we are pleased to welcome him.” “As a sitting REIT CEO, Colin offers deep, practical expertise in capital allocation, real estate investment, and operations,” said Dallas Tanner, the Company’s President and Chief Executive Officer. “He is a respected industry leader and we look forward to his contributions.” Mr. Connolly has served as President and Chief Executive Officer of Cousins since January 2019 and has more than 20 years of experience in the real estate industry. Before becoming CEO, he held other senior management positions at Cousins from 2011 to 2019. From 2004 to 2011, Mr. Connolly worked in real estate investing at Morgan Stanley, most recently as Executive Director. Prior to that, he worked at CarrAmerica Realty Corporation. Mr. Connolly graduated from Washington and Lee University and holds a Master of Business Administration from the University of Virginia’s Darden School of Business. Our purpose, Unlock the Power of Home™, reflects our commitment to address America’s housing needs by delivering high-quality living solutions and Genuine CARE™ to those who choose the flexibility and value of leasing. items.title: AI Companies Distort London Office Rents As Low-Key 'Flight To Value' Emerges
items.description: The artificial intelligence boom has supported the U.S. economy, global stock markets — and the London office market. AI firms are among the most active tenants and are paying among the top rents in London, the audience at Bisnow ’s London Office Leasing Trends and Occupier Demands event heard. And while that is not necessarily a bad thing, it does create unintended consequences for the broader market. Bisnow/Alfie Edwards Workman's Richard Taylor, Nuveen's Ilna Patel, AshbyCapital's Tom Smithers, KPF's John Bushell, Workspace's Charlie Green and Greenberg Traurig's Simon Elliott “AI companies are largely paying these very high rents. That's then setting the bar for the rest of the market and distorting the market in many ways,” Workspace CEO Charlie Green told the event, held at the 10 Emberton Walk office building, part of the new Olympia development. Maybe that trend will last, and income from AI firms will prove resilient, Green said. Maybe it won’t. “But it's just interesting how it impacts all of us,” Green said. The knock-on effect is that every office owner sees rents growing in AI-heavy buildings and areas — they are up 6% in the West End and King’s Cross so far this year and 9% in the City, according to BNP Paribas Real Estate — and thinks, “I want a piece of that,” Green said. So even if owners haven’t invested to improve buildings, they’re raising prices, Green said. That can put companies off moving, but it also presents an opportunity for owners to offer more affordable rents on good-quality older buildings. Green said there has been a shift in the London office market. In the wake of the pandemic, amenities were king, and companies desperate to get staff back to the office were willing to pay top dollar for the best-quality space. Today is different. Office space is still only a small proportion of a company’s costs, but inflation is pushing up costs, especially wages, across the board. That puts rent affordability back in the spotlight. “I think that companies are going to be thinking harder about how much they're paying and what are they getting for what they're paying,” Green said. “Perhaps we're moving away from that flight to quality that everybody talked about post-pandemic, and perhaps now we're moving into a flight to value.” Amenities and prime space are also prioritised less in a weaker job market, as employers have more leverage to order employees back to the office. “Whereas before, amenity was No. 1, and CEOs and C-suites willing to pay for it, I think that's now coming lower in the agenda because that power has probably now shifted from employees to employers,” Nuveen Director Ilna Patel said. The eternal truism of property is coming back to the fore — location is a key driver for occupiers. If a business is in a vibrant area, full of gyms and cafes, they don’t necessarily have to pay to have that in the office. More prosaic elements like good-quality WiFi are now coming above amenities that might be nice to have but are not deemed essential. "If you don't hit their resilience, they're not coming to you,” Patel said. “It doesn't matter how great the building is, where it is, they just won't come to you.” Continue reading this story with a free account Log in or register Related Topics: Charlie Green , Ilna Patel , Nuveen , Workspace Group

items.title: JLL Arranges $212.5M Sale of Senior Living Community in Lincolnwood, Illinois
items.description: JLL Arranges $212.5M Sale of Senior Living Community in Lincolnwood, Illinois by Kristin Harlow November 12, 2026 November 12, 2026 4 LINCOLNWOOD, ILL. — JLL Capital Markets has arranged the $212.5 million sale and financing of The Carrington at Lincolnwood, a 383-unit senior living community in Lincolnwood. JLL’s national seniors housing capital markets team represented the seller, a partnership of LAMB Properties, Harbert South Bay Partners and its capital partners. Senior Resource Group (SRG) and Nuveen Real Estate purchased the property. JLL arranged a five-year acquisition loan through a national bank on behalf of the buyers. The transaction represents one of the largest single-asset senior living sales nationally in 2026 and marks SRG’s entry into the Chicago market, according to JLL. SRG will assume management responsibilities from Momentum Senior Living. Built in 2018, The Carrington at Lincolnwood features two interconnected four-story buildings with 251 independent living units, 88 assisted living units and 44 secured memory care units. Amenities include an indoor pool, movie theater, wellness gym, sports bar, game room with billiards, a salon, café and bistro, libraries with computer stations, a creative arts studio, worship areas, indoor garage parking and a dog park. items.title: Renters comfortably affording a house would need a $14,408 raise to buy one (October Rent Report)
items.description: Renters comfortably affording a house would need a $14,408 raise to buy one (October Rent Report) Rental demand is up 22% as buying a single-family home stretches the budget far further than renting one. Written by Kara Ng on November 12, 2026 A household that can comfortably afford to rent a single-family home would need a $14,408 annual raise to afford the monthly costs of owning a home. Rental demand is up 22.1% year over year nationwide, as measured by the Zillow Observed Renter Demand Index, with demand for single-family rentals up 24.3%. The typical U.S. single-family rent was $2,243 a month in October, up 3.2% from a year ago, while the typical multifamily rent was $1,744, up 2.5%, according to the Zillow Observed Rent Index. Wanting a more suburban lifestyle — the extra space, yard and private garage that often come with a single-family home — doesn’t always mean stretching the budget to buy. In fact, it’s a stretch most families aren’t prepared to make, especially when a household comfortably affording the rent for a single-family home would need a $14,408 pay raise to cover the monthly costs of owning one, even before saving for a down payment. Nationally, the typical single-family rent is $2,243 a month, compared with $2,603 a month to own a single-family home with 20% down, or $360 more each month. To comfortably afford those costs — the rule of thumb being to spend no more than 30% of its income on housing — a household needs an income of $89,724 to rent and $104,132 to buy. For many households, renting a house is a choice and not a fallback. It takes less income than owning, and it leaves more room in the monthly budget. The size of the raise depends on the market The pay raise needed to buy is now the highest since early 2025, more than double the $6,463 it took in February 2026, when mortgage rates briefly fell below 6%. The gap looks very different from market to market. It’s largest in San Jose, where the income needed to buy ($404,925) is more than double the income needed to rent ($190,561), a gap of $214,364. The next largest gap is in San Francisco ($139,353), followed by San Diego ($84,101), New York ($78,208) and Los Angeles ($78,003). The smallest annual gaps are in Pittsburgh ($2,554), Houston ($4,500) and Cincinnati ($4,774). Buffalo is the only market where buying would not require a raise. Even with such a raise, would-be buyers still face another hurdle: saving a 20% down payment. About 30% of mortgage buyers use a gift or loan from family or friends, and 46% draw on two or more sources, including the use of down payment assistance programs , according to Zillow’s 2026 Consumer Housing Trends Report . In addition to the monthly cost, households deciding between renting and buying should weigh the upfront costs of buying, the chance to build equity and the opportunity for renters to invest their down payment instead. Zillow’s rent vs. buy research puts the national break-even timeline — the number of years a household would need to own before buying comes out ahead — at 7.8 years with 20% down. Rental demand keeps climbing As renting a house becomes an increasingly better value, more shoppers are turning to rentals. Rental demand is up 22.1% year over year nationwide, according to the Zillow Observed Renter Demand Index (ZORDI). Demand for single-family rentals is up 24.3%, roughly double the 12.1% rise for multifamily rentals. Rental demand surges in the Bay Area and the Sun Belt Demand rose the most in San Jose, where ZORDI is up 78.9% from a year ago, followed by San Francisco (60.5%), Austin (59.6%), Miami (51.5%) and Jacksonville (47.9%). San Jose and San Francisco are also among the markets where buying is furthest out of reach, and where rents are rising quickly, up 8.9% and 12.2% respectively. In Austin, Miami and Jacksonville, rent growth is more moderate, at 1.1%, 2.1% and 2.6%. Not every market is following the national trend. ZORDI is down year over year in Providence (-4.3%), Richmond (-1.9%), Baltimore (-1.7%), Hartford (-1.3%) and Washington, D.C. (-0.9%). WASHINGTON (November 12, 2026) – Existing-home sales decreased by 5.5% month-over-month and decreased by 8.8% year-over-year, according to the National Association of REALTORS® Existing-Home Sales report. The report provides the real estate ecosystem, including agents, homebuyers and sellers, with data on the level of home sales, price and inventory. Month-over-month sales declined in the Midwest, South and West and held steady in the Northeast. Year-over-year sales declined in all four regions. “Home buying is difficult when mortgage rates have climbed to their highest levels since 2000, aside from a single month in 2023. As a result, home sales fell to their lowest level since August 2010,” said NAR Chief Economist Lawrence Yun. “Despite fewer transactions in October, the 88 million homeowners across the country are largely in a comfortable financial position due to sizable housing wealth accumulation. The number of distressed property sales remains historically low at only 2% of all transactions,” Yun said. “Based on the current underwhelming home sales pace at a time of consistent job growth, there could be sizable pent-up demand if mortgage rates decline.” National Snapshot Total Existing-Home Sales for October Existing-home sales decreased 5.5% month-over-month. 1 Existing-home sales decreased 8.8% year-over-year to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 3.75 million. Inventory in October Total housing inventory was 1.59 million units, up 1.3% from September and 4.6% from October 2025. 2 Unsold inventory represented a 5.1-month supply, up from 4.7 months in September and 4.4 months in October 2025. Median Sales Price in October The median existing-home price for all housing types was $416,700. 3 The median price increased 0.4% from $414,900 one year ago, marking the 40th consecutive month of year-over-year price increases. Housing Affordability in October The Housing Affordability Index registered at 100.7, down from 107.3 one year ago. Year-over-year, affordability declined in all four regions. The median home price was $421,900, up 0.4% from one year ago. Condominiums and Co-ops in October Sales decreased 2.9% month-over-month to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 340,000. Sales were down 10.5% from one year ago. The median price was $365,100, up 0.3% from October 2025. Regional Snapshot for Existing-Home Sales in October Northeast Sales were unchanged month-over-month at an annual rate of 470,000. Sales were down 4.1% from October 2025. The median price was $519,600, up 3.2% from October 2025. Midwest Sales decreased 3.2% month-over-month to an annual rate of 900,000. Sales were down 8.2% year-over-year. The median price was $324,300, up 1.5% from October 2025. South Sales decreased 6.5% month-over-month to an annual rate of 1.73 million. Sales were down 8% from October 2025. items.title: Freddie Mac rates dip again this week, but sticky inflation could erase the relief
items.description: Freddie Mac rates dip again this week, but sticky inflation could erase the relief By Jiayi Xu Nov 12, 2026 What happened to mortgage rates this week? The Freddie Mac 30-year mortgage rate declined 7 basis points to 7.11% this week, its fourth straight weekly decline. Even so, it remains 87 basis points above a year ago, and the downtrend trend could potentially reverse next week as the 10-year yield returns to 5%. The strong October jobs report showed the labor market holding up well, clearing the way for the Fed’s next rate hike. On Tuesday morning, before the CPI release, Fed Governor Christopher Waller said a larger 50-basis-point move should be considered in December’s meeting if inflation came in hot. Shortly afterward, the October CPI report came in hotter than forecast, pushing the 10-year Treasury yield toward 5%. A December hike is now essentially priced in. The debate is no longer if the Fed hikes, but how far and how fast. What does this mean for the housing market? Today’s homebuyers are squeezed by both high mortgage rates and high inflation, and inflation is the bigger long-term problem. High rates raise monthly payments and shrink the loan a buyer can qualify for, and the recent pullback in pending sales shows how sensitive buyers are . But persistent high inflation is what keeps the Fed hiking and rates elevated. Inflation also leaves households with less to put toward a home, especially when wages lag prices. First-time buyers feel it most. With no equity to lean on, they must save a down payment from budgets already stretched thin. Even if rates ease, living costs rising faster than pay will keep weighing on demand for years.

items.description: Weekly Housing Trends: U.S. Market Update (Week Ending Nov. 7, 2026) By Hannah Jones Nov 12, 2026 Welcome to this weekly housing trends update, where we bring you the latest snapshot of inventory trends, listing activity, and buyer-seller dynamics across the U.S. housing market. In addition to our monthly housing trends reports , which offer deeper insights into long-term patterns, we publish these weekly updates to provide more timely views into market changes. This effort began in response to rapid shifts in the economy and housing landscape. You can count on a new Weekly Housing Trends update, fresh weekly data each Thursday, and a weekly video from our economists to help you stay informed. What this week’s data shows Though mortgage rates have fallen for the last three consecutive weeks, they remain in 7%+ territory, impacting both buyer and seller willingness to participate in the market. items.description: Existing Home Sales Hit 16-year Low By Danielle Hale Nov 12, 2026 October 2026 existing-home sales Existing home sales set an unwelcome record in October, dropping to 3.75M, their lowest since August 2010 (3.68M). This was 8.8% behind the year ago sales pace (4.11M) and also 5.5% behind September’s downwardly revised pace of 3.97M (initially reported pace was 3.99M). Mortgage rates were relatively flat near 6.7% in August, but climbed in September, especially in the second half of the month, when many of these closed sales likely would have been in contract. Although mortgage rates averaged ‘just’ 6.86% in September, lower than the 7.33% average for October, these were the highest rates of 2026 at the time, and they likely derailed some homebuying plans. I don’t think this is a new normal for home sales. Instead, it reflects a perfect storm of an abrupt shift in the financial environment and large uncertainties in the pre-election period for both policy and the economy just as the housing market usually slows for the season. While they won’t last long-term, these challenges are likely to keep home sales near long-time lows for the next few months. NAR’s pending home sales set a series record low in September dropping just (7.3%) from August, and trailing the prior year by a double-digit gap (11.3%). Meanwhile, Realtor.com October pending home sales also dropped by double-digits , signaling a rough patch for existing home sales. This rough patch coincides with mortgage rates reaching a high of 7.40%. Fortunately, the 10-year Treasury yield has pulled back from its early October highs, which has helped nudge mortgage rates below this recent peak. However, several factors are likely to put a floor under how low rates can go, including a strong economy and jobs market , persistent inflation , and an expected need for tighter monetary policy in the near term combined with sizable demand for capital from both governments and private companies, largely to finance AI-related investments. Put simply, I expect to see more homebuyers come back into the market as we move away from recent mortgage rate highs, but the upside will be limited. Rising Inventory and Slower Sales Keep Months Supply Elevated Interestingly, months supply was revised slightly lower, to 4.7 months in September as unsold inventory was revised down (now 1.57M from 1.60M), but the slower October sales pace and a modest increase in unsold inventory (1.59M) pushed months its highest pace since November 2015, tying that month’s 5.1 months of supply. Realtor.com data show that even though new listings pulled back in October , active inventory continues to rise. First-time Home Buyers Lose Ground Perhaps unsurprisingly as high-rates cut into affordability, the first-time home buyer share gave up recent gains, slipping to 29% from 31% in September and 32% one year ago. Even though higher mortgage rates keep many existing-homeowners locked-in , the equity that homeowners have accumulated is at a record high , creating opportunities for cash buying, which rose to 29% from 27% in September, tying the year ago share. Home Prices Rose Modestly Amid softer sales, the median home sales prices increased modestly, rising just 0.4% compared to last year to $416,700. The typical U.S. asking price has been softer in 2026 according to Realtor.com data, lagging behind by 2.2% in October . Regionally, sales declines from a year ago were sizable and widespread ranging from 4% to nearly 15%. In the month of October declines were more limited in the inventory-constrained and competitive Northeast (flat in October) and Midwest (-3.2%) compared to the South (-6.5%) and West (-9.7%). Pricing trends mirror sales, with home prices climbing in the Northeast (3.2%) and Midwest (1.5%) while holding steady in the West and slipping slightly in the South (-0.4%).

Rents increased in 24 of the metro's 33 submarkets, after just a handful of areas posted gains during the same period last year. The PMMS results are based on data from our Loan Product Advisor (LPA): mortgage rates collected from thousands of loan applications submitted to Freddie Mac from lenders across the country when a borrower applies for a mortgage. For more detailed information, see Enhanced Mortgage Rate Survey Explained . How is the national average determined? We collect the mortgage rate of all purchase applications based on PMMS criteria and a national average mortgage rate is calculated out of all the selected loan applications. The criteria include weekly conventional, single-family originations with conforming loan limits as set by FHFA. Is the PMMS rate based on current lender quotes or recent settlements? PMMS rates are based on applications submitted to Freddie Mac for the given week from lenders across the country. What type of lenders are included in the PMMS? Currently, our lenders are a mix of credit unions, commercial banks and mortgage lending companies. Do the PMMS results represent the rates charged on a specific day of the week? If so, which day? Or are they the average rate charged that week? PMMS is published each Thursday at noon ET. When a U.S. holiday falls on a Thursday, the PMMS will publish on the Wednesday of that week. The week of application activity starts at 12:00 a.m. ET the prior Thursday and lasts through 11:59 p.m. ET Wednesday. Therefore, the PMMS results are an average of loan rates offered Thursday through Wednesday. See our publication calendar . Why are adjustable rates no longer published? ARMs indexed to alternatives to U.S. Treasury securities have become more prevalent in the market. As we worked on enhancing the PMMS , we carefully considered which loan products were most popular for the PMMS borrower profile (good/excellent credit, 20% loans, home purchase loans on owner occupied 1-unit single-family properties). Additionally, in recent years the mortgage market has been dominated by fixed mortgage products. While there has been an uptick recently in the share of adjustable-rate mortgages (ARMs) for the broader mortgage market, ARMs remain most popular for higher loan size (nonconforming) loans. Why are fees/points no longer published? Under the current LPA requirements, fees and points are not always required to be provided by lenders. Therefore, we are not able to report on the average fees and points. How has PMMS changed over time? Since April 1971, Freddie Mac shared the average 30-year fixed-rate mortgage rate with the PMMS. We have updated the information we collect and the process for gathering data over time. Changes in Data Processes When it was launched, PMMS surveyed lenders on the rates and points for their most popular 30-year fixed-rate, 15-year fixed-rate and 5/1 hybrid amortizing adjustable-rate mortgage products. The survey was based on first-lien prime conventional conforming home purchase mortgages with a loan-to-value of 80 percent. In addition, the adjustable-rate mortgage (ARM) products were indexed to U.S. Treasury yields, and lenders were asked for both the initial coupon rate and points as well as the margin on the ARM products. Lenders surveyed each week were a mix of lender types — credit unions, commercial banks and mortgage lending companies — roughly proportional to the level of mortgage business that each type commands nationwide. On November 17, 2022, the mortgage rate gathering process was updated. Instead of surveying lenders, we now use data from our Loan Product Advisor (LPA). items.description: ATTOM Reveals July as Best Month to Buy a Home Based on Lowest Premium above AVM by ATTOM Team | Nov 12, 2026 | Home Sales & Prices , Real Estate News - Recent Articles July and November Offer Lowest Homebuying Premiums; December 24th Is the Lowest Single Day IRVINE, Calif. — Nov. 12, 2026 — ATTOM , the leading provider of property data , AI-powered intelligence , and real estate analytics solutions, today released its annual analysis highlighting the best days and months of the year to purchase a home. The report found that July offers the lowest premium of any month at 6.3 percent above market value, followed by November at 7.4 percent. Additionally, December 24 stands out as the single best day to buy a home. According to ATTOM’s latest analysis of more than 48 million single-family home and condo sales over the past 10 years, buyers who close on December 24 are seeing the lowest premium above the automated valuation model (AVM). While still above market value, homebuyers are only paying a 3.2 percent premium, compared to the 14.5 percent premium buyers are seeing on May 27, the highest of any day that occurs every year. (Full methodology is enclosed below.) Other days of the year offering lower premiums for homebuyers include: July 10 (3.5 percent premium above market value); July 9 (4.1 percent premium); July 3 (4.3 percent premium); July 2 (4.3 percent premium); and July 17 (4.6 percent premium). In total, nine of the ten lowest-premium days of the year fall in July. ATTOM’s latest analysis also looked at the best months to buy at the national level and best months to buy at the state level. Best Months to Buy Nationally, the best months to buy are July (6.3 percent premium above market value); November (7.4 percent premium); October (7.8 percent premium); September (8.2 percent premium); and December (8.2 percent premium). Best Months to Buy by State According to the study, Hawaii (-1.8 percent in January) and Michigan (-1.7 percent in November) are the only states where buyers saw a discount below full market value in their best month. Buyers in three other states paid close to market value at their best time of year: Connecticut (0.0 percent in January); Minnesota (0.0 percent in December); and Illinois (0.1 percent premium in November). Powering Real Estate Businesses with Property Data and Analytics Solutions For Every Industry Methodology For this analysis ATTOM looked at any calendar day in the last 10 years (2016 to 2025) with at least 10,000 single family home and condo sales. There were 362 days (including leap year data) that matched these criteria, with the four exceptions being Jan. 1, July 4, Nov. 11, and Dec. 25. To calculate the premium or discount paid on a given day, ATTOM compared the median sales price for homes with a purchase closing on that day with the median automated valuation model (AVM) for those same homes at the time of sale. The premium is the percentage by which the median sales price exceeds the median AVM. A negative figure is a discount. items.description: Monthly Mortgage Payments Fall to Lowest Level in 6 Weeks as Home Prices Keep Dipping Published on November 12th, 2026 by Dana Anderson Pending home sales held steady from a week earlier as prices and mortgage rates fell–but rates have since ticked back up. What to know about the U.S. housing market for the four weeks ending November 8: Home-sale prices fell for the fourth week in a row. The median home-sale price was $388,613, down 0.9% year over year. items.title: Why the 2026 fake foreclosure crisis never happened
items.description: The 2026 foreclosure crisis that some people predicted has failed to materialize, and now those people look silly. We should be thankful for the regulations and laws enacted that laid the foundation for such a sound housing credit market: The 2005 bankruptcy reform law and the 2010 Dodd-Frank laws that established qualified mortgage guidelines were historically positive for the U.S. economy. Looking at the New York Fed's Household Debt and Credit Report for Q3, we can clearly see that the anticipated foreclosure crisis hasn't happened. All the headlines showing a high percentage of year-over-year growth in foreclosure data didn’t amount to anything near a crisis. For those who expected a situation worse than what we experienced in 2008, it has been an embarrassing year. This highlights the dangers of listening to economic discussions from those without the necessary expertise. So let’s talk about where these doomers get it wrong. The idea that the FHA foreclosure moratorium, which ended in October 2025, would lead to a surge in distressed listings has been a popular topic this year. It's gotten a lot of headlines, but has fallen flat on its face, since that isn’t how the foreclosure-to-listing process works in America. At minimum, it takes 9-18 months from the start of the foreclosure process to finally add that supply to the marketplace. And foreclosure data has not, at any point since 2014, shown any material sign of credit stress building up in the pipeline. Always remember, 1%-4% of all mortgages are always going to be in delinquency; it’s when that data breaks above historical norms that it should get everyone’s attention. To illustrate what a true foreclosure crisis might look like, we can consider the historical context: since World War II, we have experienced 13 recessions with an average unemployment rate of 7.8%, but only one significant foreclosure crisis, which was the run-up to the 2008 Great Recession. It took four years for the foreclosure credit market to build up before the 2008 recession hit. As we finish Q3 of 2026, we still haven't returned to pre-COVID levels of foreclosure credit stress, as the data below has always shown for anyone who believes in reading. The New York Fed foreclosure credit stress data line moves slowly, and unless this index is above 200, there isn't much activity out of the norm. The many posts this year predicting a foreclosure crisis have proven to be exaggerated. The scale of the situation is small, and it's clear that many commentators lack the experience to accurately discuss the current market conditions. Additionally, I want to highlight HousingWire’s new listing data . During the previous housing crisis, credit foreclosures directly impacted new listing data, pushing weekly listings to between 250,000 and 400,000 — for years. These listings represented distressed sellers who were forced to sell in an underwater market. All those increases from 2005-2008 in foreclosures eventually became distressed sales, and none of that is happening today. Let's compare the new listings data for last week to the same week from 2009-2011: 2009: 280,400 new listings 2010: 353,457 new listings 2011: 352,030 new listings 2026: 54,478 new listings We're missing a credit boom/bust The 2008 massive credit boom and bust took many years to create. We have not seen this kind of credit boom in housing from 2010-2026, so it’s impossible to have a credit bust like 2008 — or "worse than 2008," as many untrained fake housing analysts have talked about for years. A lot of people can’t let go of the past, as they’re still dancing with the ghost of the 2008 housing crisis. They should relax, have a glass of wine, and reflect on their bad takes. In contrast, over the last 16 years, FICO scores in America have remained strong. Most homeowners have 30-year fixed-rate mortgages, and qualification guidelines are much more stringent and effective now. Rising wages and homeowners staying in their properties longer have contributed to the overall financial health of American households. Despite claims of an impending foreclosure crisis, the reality is quite different. In 2010, over 23% of homes in America were underwater, with loan-to-value ratios reaching nearly 86% in 2011. Currently, the loan-to-value figure is down to 44.2%, as the chart below shows. It's crucial to be cautious about who you listen to, as the narrative of a looming crisis has been overstated for many years. If someone tells you it’s housing 2008 or a foreclosure crisis is here, tell them to read a book instead of burning it, and read HousingWire. Related More: Foreclosure

items.title: Existing Home Sales Fell to 16-Year Low
items.description: Existing Home Sales Fell to 16-Year Low November 12, 2026 Fan-Yu Kuo No Comments After a brief rebound last month, existing home sales plummeted to a 16-year low in October. With mortgage rates back above 7% since mid-September and home prices still elevated, buyers continued to stay on the sidelines. Sales declined across all four regions, with the West hitting a record low while the Midwest and South fell to decade lows. As buyers wait for rate relief, homes are sitting on the market longer, resulting in for-sale inventory climbing close to pre-pandemic levels. Total existing home sales, including single-family homes, townhomes, condominiums, and co-ops, fell 5.5% to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 3.75 million in October, according to the National Association of Realtors (NAR). This marked the lowest level since August 2010. On a year-over-year basis, sales were 8.8% lower than a year ago. The existing home inventory level was 1.59 million units in October, up 1.3% from September and 4.6% from a year ago. At the current sales rate, October unsold inventory sits at a 5.1-months’ supply, up from 4.7-months in September and 4.4-months a year ago. This was the highest months' supply since November 2015. Inventory between 4.5 to 6 months’ supply is generally considered a balanced market. Homes stayed on the market for a median of 35 days in October, up from 33 days in the previous month and 34 days in October 2025. The first-time buyer share was 29% in October. The share was down from 31% in September and 32% from a year ago. The October all-cash sales share was 29% of transactions, up from 27% last month but unchanged from October 2025. All-cash buyers are less affected by changes in interest rates. The October median sales price of all existing homes was $416,700, up 0.4% from last year. This marks the 40th consecutive month of year-over-year increases. The median condominium/co-op price in October was up 0.3% from a year ago at $365,100. Recent gains for home inventory will put downward pressure on resale home prices in most markets in 2026. Existing home sales in October were mixed across the four major regions. Sales fell in the West (-9.7%), South (-6.5%) and Midwest (-3.2%), while unchanged the Northeast. On a year-over-year basis, sales decreased in all four regions, ranging from 4.1% in the Northeast to 14.5% in the West. The Pending Home Sales Index (PHSI) is a forward-looking indicator based on signed contracts. The PHSI fell from 71.2 to 66.0 in September, the lowest level since NAR began tracking in 2001. items.description: Cushman & Wakefield Named Top Ten Military Friendly® Employer for Fifth Consecutive Year, Expands Veteran Career Pathways Nationwide Phoebe Schmidt • 11/11/2026 Veteran's Day 2026 New York -- Cushman & Wakefield (NYSE: CWK) announced today that the real estate services firm has been recognized as a Top Ten Military Friendly® Employer for the fifth consecutive year. As the nation celebrates America's 250th anniversary, the firm continues expanding opportunities for veterans transitioning to civilian careers, with a particular focus on skilled trades and technical professions. "As the United States marks its 250th anniversary, we're reminded that the country's strength has always depended on people willing to serve something larger than themselves," said Bruce Mosler , Chairman of Global Brokerage. "Veterans leave the military with experience leading teams, solving problems under pressure and taking responsibility when the stakes are high. Those qualities are increasingly difficult to find and impossible to teach overnight. Creating opportunities for veterans isn't simply a way to honor their service. It's an investment in the future workforce and leadership of this country." Cushman & Wakefield employs more than 1,400 veterans across its U.S. operations and has plans to hire an additional 500 veterans this year. Through its Military & Veterans Programs, the firm provides recruitment, mentorship and career-transition support, including participation in the Department of War's SkillBridge program and military spouse employment initiatives. The firm's approach to veteran hiring and engagement has also been shared with more than 300 companies nationwide as a model for building effective post-military career pathways. The opportunity is significant. U.S. employers reported approximately 325,000 job openings in construction and 608,000 in manufacturing in July 2026, according to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics. More than 160,000 people leave military service annually with experience maintaining aircraft, vehicles, facilities, electrical systems and heavy equipment. These capabilities can translate directly to civilian careers, including building engineering, HVAC, facilities operations and project management. To help veterans and military spouses explore careers in the skilled trades, Cushman & Wakefield partnered with 50strong in September to launch the Skilled Trades Mentor Hub. The initiative connects transitioning service members, veterans and military spouses with professionals who can help them understand career options and how their experience translates to civilian roles. "Much of the conversation today is focused on AI, automation and how technology is reshaping the workforce," added Matt Disher , Executive Director, Military & Veterans Programs. "What often gets overlooked is that service members have been operating sophisticated technologies, complex systems and mission-critical equipment for years. They understand how to adapt when technology changes because they've been doing it throughout their military careers. As employers look for talent that can learn quickly, solve problems and operate in high-consequence environments, veterans are exceptionally well positioned to help lead that transformation across industries." In addition to being named a Top Ten Military Friendly® Employer for the fifth consecutive year, the firm was recently recognized as one of America's Most Patriotic Companies 2026 by Newsweek for its support of veterans, service members and military-connected communities. Institutions earning the Military Friendly® Employers designation are evaluated using both public data sources and responses from a proprietary survey. Over 1,200 companies participated in the 2026 survey. "Earning the Military Friendly® designation is more than a badge; it's a reflection of deep-rooted values and strategic foresight," said Kayla Lopez, Vice President of Memberships, Military Friendly®. "These organizations don't just open doors for veterans, spouses, and service members; they build pathways for lasting impact. Their commitment isn't performative; it's transformative. It's proof that honoring military talent is not only the right thing to do, it's the smart thing to do." moving because of housing costs, including one in three who have considered leaving the state,
according to a new survey. Yet only one in five knew that Congress recently passed federal legislation,
the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, to address affordability concerns.

The survey also found support for expanding access to single-family housing, including newly built
single-family rental homes. Among the key findings:

   ●   Affordability pressures are widespread: 85% of Raleigh-area residents say housing
       affordability is a serious problem, and 55% have considered moving because of housing costs,
       including 33% who have considered moving to another state.
   ●   Essential workers are feeling it: 67% of respondents say it is hard for teachers, nurses, police
       officers and firefighters to afford to live in the communities where they work.
   ●   Residents want housing choices, including access to single-family homes: 63% believe
       people should have access to single-family homes whether they rent or own, compared to those
       who believe they should only be available to people to own.
   ●   More residents support new rental housing than oppose it: 49% support building more new
       single-family rental homes, compared with 33% opposed.
   ●   Renters are feeling affordability pressures: 67% have considered moving because of housing
       costs, and 65% support building more new single-family rental homes.

“Housing affordability challenges are affecting communities across the country, and these results
underscore the need for more housing options. No single housing type will solve today’s housing
shortage. We need more opportunities for homeownership, more rental choices, and a continued focus
on expanding supply so families can find housing that meets their needs,” said Adrianne Todman,
President and CEO of the National Rental Home Council.

The findings come as North Carolina policymakers continue to weigh housing affordability, following
federal action addressing large institutional purchases of existing single-family homes. The 21st Century
ROAD to Housing Act limits large institutional investors from purchasing existing single-family homes
while protecting investments in preserving and building new housing, including build-to-rent homes.

Despite widespread concern about housing affordability, relatively few Raleigh-area residents are aware
of the recent federal action. For instance, only 20% of Raleigh-area residents surveyed knew Congress
had already acted to restrict large investment companies from purchasing existing single-family homes.

Asked what state lawmakers should prioritize now that federal action is in place, residents pointed first to
expanding affordable housing programs (53%), assistance for first-time homebuyers (46%) and lower
 property taxes (46%). Fewer than one in three (30%) chose additional limits on how many homes large
investment companies can own.

“In Raleigh, rising housing costs are making it harder for families to afford a home in the communities
where they live and work,” said Todman. “As North Carolina lawmakers look toward the 2027 session,
there’s an opportunity to keep working families from being priced out as the region grows.”

The survey of 600 Raleigh-area residents was conducted via Pollfish in October 2026.

items.title: AI borrowers now drive nearly half of long-dated U.S. IG issuance. PIMCO sees 3 diversifiers
items.description: Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Artificial intelligence-related borrowing is becoming a larger share of long-dated U.S. corporate debt — prompting investors to look beyond Big Tech for credit diversification. Investors could consider agency mortgage-backed securities, higher-rated private mortgage bonds and emerging market debt as credit portfolio diversifiers in a corporate debt market increasingly shaped by the AI build-out, according to Lotfi Karoui, managing director and multi-asset strategist at PIMCO. Karoui said AI-related bond issuance now weighs heavily on the broader debt market. Such borrowers now account for almost half of year-to-date gross issuance of non-financial U.S. investment-grade debt with maturities beyond 15 years, PIMCO said in a note Nov. 10. AI hyperscaler debt issuance is projected at around $250 billion in dollar-denominated bonds this year, according to Goldman Sachs forecasts. Estimates for the wider AI ecosystem debt issuance this year — which includes chipmakers, utilities and data center developers — range between $300 billion and $570 billion. There are growing concerns about an AI build-out slowdown prompted by the Democrats' sweeping victory in the U.S. midterm elections, which could pose a headache for long-duration investors looking for diversification, particularly as longer-dated U.S. Treasurys — the traditional duration portfolio hedge — have been rattled by volatility for much of 2026. "For most of the past 3 years, the AI investment boom has been an equity story, but it is increasingly becoming a bond-market story," said Kevin Thozet, a member of Carmignac's investment committee. "The numbers are becoming too large for bonds investors to ignore." Karoui said that within corporate credit, financials offer a large pool of IG exposure with much less direct sensitivity to the AI capex cycle, while "old economy" sectors such as energy can play a similar role in high-yield (HY) markets. "Both, however, are expensive, in our view," Karoui said. "Their spreads above like-maturity Treasuries generally appear tight relative to their risk-adjusted return potential." "Instead, we see other opportunities with more favorable diversification characteristics for investors wary of AI-related investment themes." Agency mortgage-backed securities Mortgage-backed securities backed by U.S. home loans guaranteed by government-sponsored enterprises like Freddie Mac and Fannie Mae have proved more resilient to higher rates and rate volatility this year compared with 2023, Karoui said. The note referenced PIMCO and Bloomberg data highlighting a 33-basis-point pickup in agency MBS over U.S. investment-grade corporate spreads as of Nov. 5, but without the same exposure to corporate borrowers. "In the U.S., high-quality securitized products such as agency mortgage-backed securities and non-agency residential MBS may provide meaningful uncorrelated exposure to the AI theme while still offering decent excess carry versus the broader investment grade market," Karoui said. Higher-rated private mortgage bonds PIMCO also pointed to senior, AAA-rated portions of bonds backed by mortgages that do not qualify for the Qualified Mortgage category under federal ability-to-repay rules. Here, Karoui said that in AAA-rated non-qualified mortgage tranches, the "potential benefits likely outweigh risks." Specifically, the risk stems more from repayments taking longer than expected, rather than the risk that borrowers will fail to pay. That risk has pushed returns higher, while certain newer deals are structured to repay senior investors more quickly and offer protection against losses. "We think the repricing in AAA non-QM creates an intriguing opportunity," Karoui said. "Wider spreads largely compensate investors for extension risk and structural risk tied to materially higher expected credit losses, and today's new issues embed better mitigations against those risks than earlier deals." Emerging market debt Bonds issued by emerging market governments and companies offer another diversification play to U.S. Big Tech. "Although there are pockets of EM with meaningful AI exposure, notably South Korea and Taiwan, much of that is an equity story rather than a fixed income one," said Karoui. "For bond portfolios, EM debt therefore remains a relatively differentiated source of yield, duration, and country-specific risk." He zeroed in on U.S. dollar-denominated emerging market investment-grade "semi-liquid" bond deals — used to finance infrastructure investment — noting they have offered a median pickup of around 40 basis points this year compared to plain vanilla EM bonds. He also flagged opportunities beyond the main benchmarks, including in commodity-exporting countries, while noting that in local-currency bonds, exchange-rate swings can add to returns or erode them. "To be clear, it is not that EM is a lower-risk asset class. Rather, it is that EM debt is exposed to a mix of political, fiscal, and monetary forces that are different than the risks facing the domestic U.S. market," Karoui said. items.title: Federal Reserve Board announces pricing, effective January 1, 2027, for payment services the Federal Reserve Banks provide to banks and credit unions, and changes to streamline and adjust their check services
items.description: Federal Reserve Board announces pricing, effective January 1, 2027, for payment services the Federal Reserve Banks provide to banks and credit unions, and changes to streamline and adjust their check services For release at 1:30 p.m. EST Share --> --> --> --> --> --> The Federal Reserve Board on Thursday announced pricing, effective January 1, 2027, for payment services the Federal Reserve Banks provide to banks and credit unions, such as the clearing of checks, automated clearing house (ACH) transactions, instant payments, and wholesale payment and settlement services. By law, the Federal Reserve must establish fees to recover the costs, including imputed costs, of providing payment services over the long run. The Federal Reserve expects to recover 101.5 percent of actual and imputed expenses in 2027, including the return on equity that would have been earned if a private-sector firm provided the services. Overall, price changes for 2027 will result in an estimated 1.4 percent average price increase for established, mature services. In addition, the Federal Reserve Banks announced changes to streamline and adjust their check services. As described in the request for information on check services issued last year, the volume of checks processed by the Federal Reserve Banks is declining, but checks remain an important payment instrument for many consumers and businesses. The changes were informed by public feedback and ensure that the Federal Reserve Banks continue to provide check services efficiently. The adjustments include optimizing check processing windows during low-volume periods, increasing fees that banks and credit unions pay to process checks, and other operational updates. These changes do not impact consumers' and businesses' ability to pay with or receive checks and only impact how banks and credit unions process checks with Federal Reserve Banks. The entire 2027 fee schedule for all of the Federal Reserve's payment services is published on FRBservices.org ® . Additional information on the Federal Reserve's payments services, including service usage statistics, is available on the Board's website . For media inquiries, please email [email protected] or call 202-452-2955. Board memo (PDF) Federal Register notice (PDF) Last Update: November 12, 2026

items.description: Live Poll The corner stall just inside the entrance of The Market at Dallas Farmers Market is between lives. For nearly a decade, it belonged to Caribbean Cabana, the Jamaican restaurant relocating to another space nearby. Soon, it will become the first permanent home of Insurgent. A few weeks ago, I met Insurgent’s married chefs Sam and Gabby Lopez at a table facing their future home. At the time, a crew was hard at work preparing for the opening and hoisting the new signage for Insurgent into place so that it hung correctly. The duo built Insurgent from a Denton food trailer that, Sam jokes, “swayed if someone moved too quickly inside.” Now they are preparing for a permanent kitchen that will allow chef’s counter dinners and the kind of culinary experiences that four wheels (and unpredictable equipment) would not always support. On paper, they’re beyond prepared. Both graduated from the Culinary Institute of America, and their combined resumes include The French Laundry and Bouchon Bakery, two of the most recognizable names in American fine dining. Each of the chefs has accumulated the technique, discipline, and pedigree expected to construct serious culinary careers. Despite those lengthy accomplishments, they still arrived at the 2024 event that changed their careers forever with $28 in the bank. Gabby woke up and checked their account but because it was the first of the month, they had made an automatic payment for their commissary kitchen. They had already spent nearly their last dollar preparing for the Food Truck Championship of Texas in Graham , west of Fort Worth. While Sam pondered canceling their participation, Gabby was more optimistic. “What’s the worst that’s going to happen?” she remembers saying. “We already signed up. We’ve got to stick to our word.” Luckily, they loaded the trailer and served the sandwich that would eventually win the 2024 Texas Food Truck Grand Champion title: shaved prime rib layered with house-made buttermilk dressing, red wine-braised cabbage and onions, garlic butter, and jus made from the trimmings. By the end of the day, that sandwich earned the Lopezes a $10,000 check, an oversized wrestling-style championship belt, and enough bookings to carry their business for months. So, of course, it had to make an appearance on their new menu. When he did enroll in culinary classes in high school, it was for more practical reasons than anything else. Planning his future life, he just wanted to know how to feed himself. As it turned out, he was pretty good at it. items.title: GAMLS: Home prices increase despite overall market slowdown
items.description: GAMLS: Home prices increase despite overall market slowdown by John Yellig November 12, 2026 Via Georgia MLS. The median sales price for an Atlanta-area home rose 1.3% year over year to $395,000 in October despite other market metrics showing signs of a cooling market, Georgia MLS said in its Housing Market Snapshot . Closed and pending sales, as well as new listings, all declined as active listings increased. “October's housing data tells us that buyers haven't necessarily left the market; they're simply taking longer to make a decision," GAMLS Chief Marketing Officer John Ryan said. "We are seeing buyer caution translate into fewer closed transactions, all while home prices remain relatively stable. This is a market where value has replaced urgency, and consumer confidence will play an increasingly important role in determining when buyers are ready to move forward." The number of homes sold fell 19.5% year over year and 4.3% month over month to 3,735 residences, while pending sales, which indicate future closings, dropped 26.8% from 2025 and 6.4% from September to 3,332 for the 10th consecutive month of annual declines. New listings fell 8.8% annually and 4.3% monthly to 7,788 homes; active listings rose 1.4% from October 2025 and 1.2% from September to 21,919. "Buyers have more choices and are taking the time to evaluate their options, which means sellers cannot rely on the urgency we saw in more competitive markets," Ryan said. "Pricing a home appropriately from the outset, demonstrating its value and making sure it stands out are critical. Properties that are positioned realistically for current market conditions will be better positioned to attract buyer interest." Georgia MLS’ 12-county report includes Cherokee, Clayton, Cobb, Dekalb, Douglas, Fayette, Forsyth, Fulton, Gwinnett, Henry, Paulding and Rockdale counties. items.description: The Generational Housing Divide: Millennials Had It Better Than Baby Boomers–Until the Pandemic Changed the Math Published on November 12th, 2026 by Dana Anderson , Yingqi Xu and Szu Yu Chen Timing made a big difference for millennials. Those who bought a home before 2022 locked in historically low mortgage rates. But those who bought after rates and prices surged spent about 35% of their income on housing–and many other millennials were priced out entirely. Baby boomers had a brutal start, with double-digit mortgage rates in the early 1980s, but falling rates gave them decades to refinance. When boomers were in their late 30s, they spent just over 25% of their income on housing. The typical monthly payment was about $3,000 when elder millennials were 40 to 44 (2021 to 2025), versus about $1,986 for boomers at those ages, in today’s dollars. Millennials earn more than boomers did at the same age in today’s dollars, partly because more women are in the workforce, but housing costs more than cancel out the difference. If millennials hadn’t spent so much money on avocado toast, they’d all own their dream home by now–right? Wrong. Just over half of millennials own their home . For the rest, housing costs have soared so much in recent years that skipping the avocado toast in their 20s wouldn’t have made a dent. The story isn’t about constant struggle, though–it’s about timing. Elder millennials who bought a home in their early 30s had it better than baby boomers did at the same age: Historically low mortgage rates and higher household incomes meant those millennials spent about 27% of their income on housing at age 30, compared with 36% for boomers. Then the pandemic changed the math. Mortgage rates jumped from around 3% to nearly 7%, and home prices surged. Since rates rose above 6% in 2022, elder millennials have spent up to 35% of their income on monthly mortgage payments, compared with roughly 25% for boomers at the same age–even though millennials earn more, adjusted for inflation. Boomers might point out that mortgage rates were much higher in their day. They’d be right: Rates peaked at over 16% in 1981 and stayed in double digits for much of the decade. But prices were lower. In the 1980s, when many boomers were in their 30s, the typical U.S. home sold for about $235,000 to $265,000 in today’s dollars. When elder millennials reached the same age–prime homebuying age–in the 2010s and 2020s, typical prices ranged from about $275,000 to $455,000. Key takeaway: Buying at the wrong time was painful for both generations, but boomers had a better chance to recover. Falling rates throughout the late 1980s, 1990s and early 2000s gave them many opportunities to refinance into lower payments. Millennials who bought before 2022 secured historically low mortgages; those who bought later—or never managed to buy—face a much less forgiving market. Of course, it’s possible the market could become more forgiving for millennials over time; rates may eventually fall significantly enough that many millennials have the opportunity to refinance into lower payments. This is based on an analysis of Redfin and U.S. Census data. A few notes to help contextualize the numbers: All dollar figures are adjusted for inflation. Much of the data illustrates each generation’s typical experience at a given age, combining everyone in that generation who has reached that age, whenever that happened for them. Because millennials are still aging into their 40s, for example, our 40-to-44 figures only capture the oldest millennials, who hit those ages between 2021 and 2025. All boomers have been through that age range, so their figures include the whole generation. Please see the end of this report for a detailed methodology. Millennials Had an Early Homebuying Advantage In their early 30s, elder millennials who bought a home spent a smaller share of their income on housing than boomers did at the same age, despite much higher home prices. Imagine a median-earning millennial born in 1984 who bought a home at age 30. They would have spent around 27% of their income to purchase the typical home, within the “don’t spend more than 30% of your income on housing costs” rule of thumb. Two factors helped: cheap borrowing and higher household incomes. Millennials benefited from roughly a decade of historically low mortgage rates; they fell below 3% in 2021. Millennials also tend to have higher household incomes than boomers did at the same age. At age 37, the typical elder millennial household earned an average of $100,000, compared with $88,000 when boomers were that age. The discrepancy is partly because two-income households are more common today. About 78% of women participate in the U.S. workforce, up from roughly 60% in 1980. It’s also worth noting that millennials typically work similar hours for more money than baby boomers at the same life stage. Then the Math Changed The millennial advantage didn't last. Mortgage rates jumped from around 3% in late 2021 to nearly 7% in late 2022, after home prices had surged about 40% nationwide during the pandemic homebuying frenzy. Rising rates often cool prices, but this time, prices didn’t fall. That mix of high prices and mortgage rates that had doubled from their pandemic-era low meant Americans had to spend a much higher share of their income to buy a home. Imagine that same millennial, born in 1984: If they bought a home at age 40 instead of 30, their housing costs shot up to about 35% of their income. items.title: Just 3 Major U.S. Metros Are Seller’s Markets–the Fewest Since the Pandemic Freeze
items.description: Just 3 Major U.S. Metros Are Seller’s Markets–the Fewest Since the Pandemic Freeze Published on November 12th, 2026 by Dana Anderson There are just 3 seller’s markets among the 50 most populous U.S. metros, and they’re all in the Northeast: Nassau County, NY, Newark, NJ and Montgomery County, PA. Nationwide, house hunters had more negotiating power in October than at any point since at least 2013, with 71% more home sellers than buyers. The number of buyers in the market fell to a new record low, while the number of sellers rose to its highest level since March 2020. 41 of the 50 most populous U.S. metro areas are buyer’s markets, led by Miami, Nashville and Las Vegas. Just three of the 50 most populous U.S. metro areas were seller’s markets in October. That’s tied for the fewest in records dating back to 2016, matching April 2020, when the pandemic froze the housing market. Nassau County, NY was the number-one seller’s market, with 24.7% fewer sellers than buyers. The other seller’s markets were Newark, NJ (-14.3%) and Montgomery County, PA (-12.1%). All three seller’s markets became less strong seller’s markets in October. In Nassau County, there were 28.3% fewer sellers than buyers in September, a bigger gap than October’s 24.7%. Newark’s gap shrunk from 17.6% to 14.3%, and Montgomery County’s shrunk from 20.1% to 12.1%. Milwaukee, which was a seller’s market in September, is now balanced, meaning it doesn’t favor sellers or buyers. The seller’s markets are places where limited homebuilding has kept housing supply tight. In the greater New York City area, combine that with strong demand for homes near a major job center, and buyers are competing for homes. Home-sale prices rose an average of 3.3% year over year across the three seller’s markets in October. That’s compared with a 0.3% uptick across all of the buyer’s markets, a sign that in seller’s markets, competition among buyers is pushing up home prices. “Buyers looking in these pockets of the Northeast should be prepared for a very different experience than buyers elsewhere in the country,” said Redfin Senior Economist Asad Khan . “They may have less room to negotiate, especially on desirable, move-in-ready homes, and could face multiple-offer situations. If you're shopping in one of these markets, it's especially important to know your budget, be ready to act when the right home comes along and avoid getting swept up in a bidding war.” Home Sellers Outnumber Buyers Nationwide By Widest Margin Since Post-Recession Financial Crisis For 6th Straight Month Seller’s markets are the exception to a national picture that heavily favors buyers. Nationwide, homebuyers have more negotiating power than at any point in Redfin’s records. There were an estimated 70.5% more home sellers than buyers in the U.S. housing market in October, the biggest gap in records dating back to 2013. That marks the sixth record-breaking month in a row, and the margin is up from 65.6% in September. The Sun Belt is driving the extreme buyer’s market nationwide, led by huge seller surpluses in Miami, Nashville, TN and Las Vegas. When sellers outnumber buyers, buyers typically have more negotiating power because they have options. That’s why a market with a lot more sellers than buyers is considered a buyer’s market. We define a market where there are over 10% more sellers than buyers as a buyer’s market and a market where there are over 10% fewer sellers than buyers as a seller’s market. A market where the gap is plus or minus 10% is considered a balanced market. We estimated the number of buyers using proprietary Redfin data on the typical time from a buyer’s first tour to close of purchase, and MLS data on active listings and pending sales. The estimated number of sellers in the market is simply the number of active listings in the MLS. These estimates are seasonally adjusted and subject to revision. See a more detailed methodology here and view an interactive dashboard here. It’s only a buyer’s market for people who can afford to buy. High housing costs and economic jitters have pushed many would-be homebuyers to back off in recent years, creating the imbalance between buyers and sellers we see today. “A buyer-friendly market can help make homeownership a little more attainable, even if it doesn't solve the affordability challenges that have kept many people on the sidelines,” Khan said. “Sellers are increasingly competing for buyers' attention, which can translate into price reductions, concessions and other savings. First-time buyers don’t have equity from a previous home to put toward a purchase, which makes saving for a down payment a big hurdle–but they also don’t have to sell a home before they can buy or give up a low mortgage rate. With a historic buyer’s market and home prices that are finally ticking down after three years of increases, first-time buyers who have been waiting–and can afford today’s costs–may have an opportunity to make a move.” Homebuyer Count Drops to New Record Low, Widening the Buyer-Seller Gap The gap between buyers and sellers widened in October because would-be buyers retreated, while sellers continued listing their homes, albeit at a sluggish pace. There were an estimated 895,752 homebuyers in the market nationwide in October, the lowest level in records dating back to 2013. That’s down 2% from a month earlier, the sixth straight monthly decline. Mortgage rates averaged 7.33% in October, up from 6.86% in September, which priced out more would-be buyers. items.title: Mortgage Rates Fall for Fourth Straight Week Despite Looming Fed Hike
items.description: Mortgage rates continued their slow retreat for a fourth consecutive week, mirroring the trajectory of bond yields, although this week's hotter-than-expected inflation print suggests the relief will be short-lived. The average rate on 30-year fixed home loans decreased to 7.11% for the week ending Nov. 12, down 7 basis points from 7.18% the week before, according to Freddie Mac . For perspective, rates averaged 6.24% one year ago. "Mortgage rates dropped to their lowest level in seven weeks, a welcome development that gives borrowers greater flexibility as they navigate the current housing market," says Sam Khater , Freddie Mac's chief economist. A month of falling mortgage rates comes as welcome news for homebuyers, though Realtor.com® senior economist Jiayi Xu warns that a reversal could come as soon as next week. The stronger-than-forecast October jobs report showed the labor market holding up well, clearing the way for the Federal Reserve's next federal funds rate hike as part of its mandate to curb inflation. Fed Gov. Christopher Waller warned this week that a larger 50-basis-point increase should be considered in December’s Federal Open Market Committee meeting if inflation remains hot. What will the Fed do? Shortly after Waller's warning, the October consumer price index report exceeded economists' expectations, pushing the 10-year Treasury yield toward 5%. A December hike is now essentially priced in, with odds of a 25-basis-point increase topping 93%, according to CME FedWatch . The odds of another quarter-percentage-point hike in January 2027 currently stand at 67%. "The debate is no longer if the Fed hikes, but how far and how fast," says Xu. Today's homebuyers find themselves squeezed by both high mortgage rates and high inflation, and Xu contends that inflation is the bigger long-term problem. "High rates raise monthly payments and shrink the loan a buyer can qualify for, and the recent pullback in pending sales shows how sensitive buyers are ," notes the economist. "But persistent high inflation is what keeps the Fed hiking and rates elevated." Crucially, inflation also erodes households' purchasing power, especially when wages lag consumer prices. In October, existing-home sales dropped to their lowest level since August 2010, according to the latest data from the National Association of Realtors® . Loading... Headwinds for buyers In this economic environment, first-time buyers are hit the hardest because they have no existing equity to use as a cushion, forcing them to save toward a down payment from already stretched budgets. "Even if rates ease, living costs rising faster than pay will keep weighing on demand for years," says Xu. Sellers have responded to cooling buyer demand by pulling back. This week, new listing activity fell 10.3% year over year after six weeks of more incremental declines, according to the latest weekly Realtor.com housing trends report . "Sellers are discouraged because of how disengaged buyers are," says Realtor.com senior economist Hannah Jones . "The prices buyers are open to are less appealing to sellers than they were when mortgage rates were lower." How your credit score affects your mortgage Your credit score plays a role when you apply for a mortgage . A credit score will determine whether you qualify for a mortgage and the interest rate you'll receive. The higher the credit score, the lower the interest rate you'll qualify for. The credit score you need will vary depending on the type of loan. A score of 620 is a "fair" rating. However, people applying for a Federal Housing Administration loan might be able to get approved with a credit score of 500, which is considered a low score. Homebuyers with credit scores of 740 or higher are typically considered to be in very good standing and can usually qualify for better rates, which can reduce monthly payments. Snejana Farberov is a reporter at Realtor.com covering the U.S. housing market and the latest domestic real estate trends. She has worked as a general assignment journalist in New York City and Long Island for 16 years, writing for New York Post, Daily Mail, and News 12. Snejana earned bachelor's degrees in journalism and Italian from St. John's University, followed by a master’s degree from Columbia University School of Journalism.

items.title: Apartment Loans Fuel A Booming CRE CLO Market Not Seen Since 2021
items.description: Demand for apartment bridge loans is pushing CRE collateralized loan obligation issuance to heights not seen since 2021. Investors bought up $40.2B worth of the debt in the first 10 months of the year, up 66% from last year by dollar volume, according to data from Trepp provided to Bisnow . But volatile debt markets have left some issuers waiting on the sidelines for now, which is likely to weigh on fourth-quarter issuance. “I think there's a number of issuers who could have come to market in Q4 but instead are acting a little slower and looking to bring their deals to market in January,” said David Henschke, managing director and head of capital markets at Benefit Street Partners , an alternative credit asset manager and CRE CLO issuer. Bisnow/created with Google Gemini Henschke forecasts a modest level of new CRE CLO issuance through the end of the year, and he suspects the total will fall short of the $45.4B record from 2021. Investors are struggling to divine the direction of interest rates and are waiting to deploy capital until after the Federal Reserve votes at its meeting in December, he said. “We'll see what the Fed does there, and then you'll have some of that uncertainty kind of behind you,” he said. It’s that same uncertainty that is driving up CRE CLO issuance in the first place. Underlying loans bundled into CRE CLOs are typically bridge or transitional debt with two- or three-year terms. The majority of CRE CLOs today are made up of loans being used to refinance existing mortgages, but the capital is also used by developers as a transitional loan for a newly completed project on its way to full occupancy and by buyers looking for short-term acquisition financing before securing a longer-dated mortgage. “What the CRE CLO market is designed to do is be a bridge facility, and that’s what it’s doing,” said Andy Boettcher, who leads research at Trepp. “It’s bridging new product that hit during a supply wave that didn’t hit its lease-up target, and it just needs time.” The CRE CLO market was built for these transitional market phases, where there’s a sudden glut of new development as the U.S. saw during the pandemic era, he said. The loans are typically floating-rate debt, which leads to higher borrowing costs when interest rates climb, and the debt has been the fastest-growing segment of the nonagency CMBS market this year, according to Morgan Stanley . https://public.flourish.studio/visualisation/30869666/visualisation.json?ref=embed-script Multifamily loans make up nearly three-quarters of all CRE CLO debt issued this year through October, and 57% of assets underwritten for CRE CLOs were built within the last five years, according to Trepp. The makeup is a shift away from the retail and office assets that were being pledged as collateral in the recent past, Morgan Stanley analysts wrote in a September research note. Office exposure made up as much as a quarter of CRE CLO collateral prior to 2020 but shrank to just 2% of issuance through this August, according to the investment bank. Some owners with maturing debt are looking at a landscape where the 10-year U.S. Treasury yield climbed above 5% before retreating and are opting to take the shorter-term CRE CLO debt as a way to effectively bet on lower debt costs within a few years. “The cost of equity, getting new equity in from somewhere else on one of these deals that has to be refinanced, is more expensive than three years of building the lease roll, stabilizing the occupancy, stabilizing the rent roll, and saying, ‘I now have a bigger value than I had going in,’” Boettcher said. But there are signs that the marketplace is itself being strained by the elevated rate environment. The CRE CLO distress rate jumped from 19% in July to 28% in August, the sharpest one-month move of any deal type this year, according to Cred iQ . Single-asset, single-borrower CMBS loans, by contrast, held flat near 22%. While climbing, the CRE CLO distress rate is concentrated in a handful of large deals, not widely dispersed. Five deals account for 38% of all of the CRE CLO special servicing balance. The distress traces to loans originated in 2021 and 2022 that now account for $3B worth of CRE CLO loans in special servicing, according to Cred iQ. Investors have shaken off the rising delinquency rates because they're concentrated in a handful of loans and because investment-grade bondholders in the segment have rarely seen real losses, Henschke said. The structure typically leaves sponsors holding the first-loss position, aligning issuers with investors, making it the most conservative structure in the CMBS market, he said. Owners opting for the shorter-term debt that comes with a CRE CLO are hoping that the interest rate environment will look better when the debt comes due in a few years. Many of the assets could refinance today with a traditional mortgage, but owners are instead taking a higher interest bill today for the prospect of greater savings in the years ahead. “You have assets that probably could go fixed-rate in today's market; they're not really bridging anything to change at the property. It's really a bridge for potentially market conditions to change,” Henschke said. Expert Quote: "Education and awareness are significant pieces of the puzzle," — Chris Birk, Vice President of Mortgage Insight, Veterans United Overview bullets generated by AI with editorial review. Mortgage lenders could have made approximately 83,100 mortgages, representing $41 billion in volume in 2025 through the Veterans Affairs mortgage guarantee program, an analysis from Veterans United Home Loans found. This was an increase from a $37.9 billion gap one year prior. The share of VA loans originated remains lower than the number of eligible borrowers in dozens of housing markets, the report claimed. Why aren't eligible borrowers seeking a VA mortgage "Education and awareness are significant pieces of the puzzle," said Chris Birk, vice president of mortgage insight at Veterans United. "Some Veterans may not fully understand the benefits they've earned, while others may be working with real estate agents who aren't as familiar with VA financing." Birk also pointed to the persistent misconceptions about VA loans which can influence how borrowers, agents and sellers approach these transactions which seek this form of financing. Past surveys, including one from Navy Federal Credit Union , showed many veterans had erroneous ideas about the VA program, including not being aware it offers 100% loan-to-value ratio mortgages. A NewDay USA survey from this past April of current or past servicemembers and reservists found that about 13% said they were extremely well educated, with 20% very well educated, about their mortgage benefit. The leading response was somewhat at 35%, followed by hardly at 19% and not well educated at all by 13%. What is the role of housing affordability in the VA use gap Part of the problem might be general affordability. Just under 8% of homes for sale as of Oct. 23 were within the reach of a veteran who earns his or her local median income, with a 100% LTV, a study from Movoto by Lower stated. The study used the then-current 7.32% average rate for a VA mortgage at 28% of median income for veterans who live in a particular metro area. Movoto found 86,277 of over 1.11 million homes listed for sale in 196 metro areas were affordable to this group; the data did not include calculations for taxes and insurance, which also impacts monthly mortgage payments. Nationwide, veterans represent 6.2% of the adult population. The largest numbers are in New York City, Washington and Dallas-Fort Worth. But the highest shares for where veterans live are in Jacksonville, North Carolina, 21.8%; Killeen-Temple, Texas, 19.2%; and Fayetteville, North Carolina, 18%. All three are where large military installations are located, Movoto said. Where are the opportunities to market VA mortgages In the Veterans United study, New York is also the largest metro for untapped VA borrowers. The study looked at estimates of potential lender opportunity for these loans, so it did not take into account veterans who used another mortgage product to purchase a home. "The geographic differences are telling," Birk said. Markets with a strong military presence, those close to bases for example, tend to have higher VA loan utilization. But in some metros with larger veteran populations, they might not have as much knowledge about the program. "That suggests awareness could be playing an important role," Birk said.
